title: How a Virtual Service Edge cluster spreads and returns traffic

prose.label: Inside the cluster.
prose.text: {{bundled-lb}} {{carp-active-passive}} {{dsr}} This is the same CARP and DSR model as the hardware cluster ([[zia.private-service-edge.cluster-architecture]]); the difference is that the customer runs it. As with the hardware cluster, the return path does not come back through the load balancer, so stateful devices between the cluster and clients must tolerate it.

prose.label: Using an external load balancer.
prose.text: Whether Zscaler recommends external load balancers at all differs between pages {{divergence:external-lb-recommendation}}. {{external-lb-clustered}} {{external-lb-standalone}} {{external-lb-probes}}

builtin-lb-benefits.statement: The VM images include a load balancer along with the Virtual Service Edge, and Zscaler recommends using the built-in load balancer, which distributes traffic on a per-session basis, monitors health and prunes Virtual Service Edges that fail health checks (adding them back when they report good health), and updates cluster members consecutively with zero downtime. Using it requires enabling Promiscuous mode on the virtualization platform, which can instead be restricted to a dedicated port group containing just the Zscaler VMs.

quotes: The virtual machine (VM) images include a load balancer (LB) along with the Virtual Service Edge. Zscaler recommends using the built-in LB.
Distributing the traffic to Virtual Service Edges on a per-session basis.
Monitoring the health of the Virtual Service Edges and pruning those that fail health checks, automatically adding them to the LB when they report good health.
Updating Virtual Service Edges in a cluster consecutively, resulting in zero downtime during updates.
Using the built-in LB requires enabling Promiscuous mode on the virtualization platform.
Promiscuous mode can instead be restricted to a dedicated port group, which contains just the Zscaler VMs.

external-lb-when.statement: If the organization's compliance requirements do not allow the required changes to the virtual switches to use the built-in load balancer, an external load balancer can be used instead.

quotes: If your organization's compliance requirements do not allow you to make the required changes to the virtual switches to use the built-in LB, an external LB can be used instead.

external-lb-clustered.statement: Of the two options the external load balancer page gives for using an external load balancer, it marks clustered Virtual Service Edges without the required switches "(Recommended)"; that label applies among the external options only. Because the instances cannot talk to each other, each assumes it is the only cluster member, becomes the primary member and owns the cluster IP. The external load balancer forwards traffic directly to the Virtual Service Edge IP (not the cluster IP), balances per session with optional Client IP persistence, and monitors the Virtual Service Edge IP address (not the cluster IP). From the cloud's point of view the instances are individual members of the same cluster, so updates occur consecutively with zero downtime.

quotes: Clustered Virtual Service Edges Without the Required Switches (Recommended)
In this mode, because the Virtual Service Edge cannot talk to each other, each one assumes that it is the only member of the cluster and becomes the primary member of the cluster.
As a result, all Virtual Service Edges in the cluster declare themselves as primary members of the cluster and own the cluster IP.
Configure your external LB to forward traffic directly to the Virtual Service Edge IP (not the cluster IP).
Monitor the Virtual Service Edge IP address (not the cluster IP).

from the cloud point of view, they are considered individual members of the same cluster. Therefore, updates occur to the Virtual Service Edges consecutively, resulting in zero downtime when the cluster is updated.
Set the load balancing method to per session basis.
(Optional) Enable Client IP based persistence.
evidence.after: Clustered Virtual Service Edges Without the Required Switches (Recommended)

external-lb-standalone.statement: Virtual Service Edges can be deployed in standalone mode with an external load balancer to distribute the load, and updates for standalone instances behind one should be scheduled to avoid downtime.

quotes: You can deploy the Virtual Service Edges in standalone mode and use an external LB to distribute the load.
Updates for Virtual Service Edges in standalone mode using an external LB should be scheduled to avoid downtime.

external-lb-probes.statement: For an external load balancer the page lists three probes to use one of: an ICMP ping to the service IP, a TCP port check to the proxy ports, and HTTP probes to an externally hosted web server via proxy, which need a suitable policy on the Virtual Service Edge to allow the probes.

quotes: Zscaler recommends using one of the following methods to monitor Virtual Service Edges using an external LB:
ICMP ping to the service IP. This will ensure services are up and running
TCP portcheck to the proxy ports
HTTP probes to an external hosted web server via proxy can also be used. This method will need a suitable policy on the Virtual Service Edge to allow the probes.

bundled-lb.statement: Each Virtual Service Edge has a load balancer bundled in, designed to distribute user traffic evenly across the Virtual Service Edges.

quotes: As shown in the diagram below, each Virtual Service Edge has a load balancer (LB) bundled in. The load balancer is specifically designed to distribute user traffic evenly across the Virtual Service Edges.

carp-active-passive.statement: The load balancers use CARP for active-passive fault tolerance: all Virtual Service Edge instances in the cluster are active, one load balancer instance is active at a time, it receives ingress traffic through the cluster IP address and directs it to the appropriate Virtual Service Edge, and if it fails the passive load balancer takes over automatically with no service disruption.

quotes: To ensure high availability, the Zscaler load balancers use the Common Address Redundancy Protocol (CARP) for active-passive fault tolerance.
all Virtual Service Edge instances in the cluster are active, and one load balancer instance is active at a time.
The active load balancer receives ingress traffic through the cluster IP address and directs the traffic to the appropriate Virtual Service Edge.
If the active load balancer fails, then the passive load balancer automatically takes over, ensuring no disruption in service.

dsr.statement: In a cluster, Virtual Service Edges run in Direct Server Return mode: requests go through the load balancer to the Virtual Service Edge, but the response flows from the Virtual Service Edge to the user, skipping the load balancer on the return.

quotes: Virtual Service Edges also run in Direct Server Return (DSR) mode. DSR allows the requests to go through the load balancer to the Virtual Service Edge, but the response flows from the Virtual Service Edge to the user, skipping the load balancer on the return.

external-lb-discouraged.statement: Zscaler does not recommend external load balancers; an organization that must use one is pointed to a separate article, Using an External Load Balancer with Virtual Service Edges.

quotes: Zscaler does not recommend using external load balancers. However, if your organization must use an external load balancer, see Using an External Load Balancer with Virtual Service Edges.

standalone-needs-external-lb-for-ha.statement: If clustering fault tolerance is required, a Standalone deployment needs an external load balancer; the specifications article notes that Virtual Service Edges with an External Load Balancer are deployed in certain situations.

quotes: If clustering fault tolerance is required, ensure to have an external load balancer for Standalone deployment.
In certain situations, the Virtual Service Edges with an External Load Balancer are deployed.

inbuilt-lb-recommended-on-esxi.statement: In the VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V environments, Zscaler recommends the in-built load balancer for Virtual Service Edges deployed in cluster mode; in public cloud environments the native cluster mode is not supported, and public cloud load balancers can provide the redundancy.

quotes: In the VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V environments, Zscaler recommends utilizing the in-built load balancer for Virtual Service Edges deployed in cluster mode.

In public cloud environments such as Microsoft Azure, AWS EC2, Microsoft Hyper-V, and GCP, the native cluster mode of deployment is not supported, and you can use public cloud load balancers to ensure redundancy between the Virtual Service Edges.

inbuilt-lb-recommended-on-esxi.conditions: Quote widened to the full sentences: the earlier quote omitted the environment qualifier and the public-cloud sentence; the statement now also says native cluster mode is unsupported there. Previously "In the VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V environments, Zscaler recommends the in-built load balancer for Virtual Service Edges deployed in cluster mode; in public cloud environments, public cloud load balancers provide the redundancy."

health-probe-firewall-rule.statement: For the load balancer's health probes to work, a Firewall Filtering rule must allow all Virtual Service Edge proxy, load balancer and cluster IP addresses as sources, with the Allow action.

quotes: Zscaler performs ICMP and HTTP monitoring from the LB to the Virtual Service Edge
For health probes to work, you must create a Firewall Filtering rule to allow all Virtual Service Edge proxy, LB, and cluster IP addresses.
In Add Firewall Filtering Rule window, click the Source IP tab.
In IP Addresses, add the following IP address for your Virtual Service Edges:
Under Network Traffic, select Allow.

esxi-vswitch-settings.statement: On ESXi, Promiscuous Mode (Accept), MAC Address Changes and Forged Transmits must be enabled on the vSwitch or port group; promiscuous mode is required because the Zscaler load balancers and Service Edges use CARP. Zscaler recommends a dedicated port group, because vSwitch-level promiscuous mode can let other VMs on the vSwitch sniff Virtual Service Edge traffic.

quotes: The Promiscuous Mode option must be enabled (i.e., set to Accept) on the vSphere switch (vSwitch) or at the port group level.
Zscaler LBs and Public Service Edges for Internet & SaaS use the Common Address Redundancy Protocol (CARP) to process traffic across multiple Public Service Edge instances.
To support this, enabling promiscuous mode on your Virtual Service Edge interfaces is required.
The MAC Address Changes option must be enabled on the vSwitch or port group.
The Forged Transmits option must be enabled on the vSwitch or port group.
Virtual Service Edges often share the vSwitch with other corporate VMs and settings applied on the vSwitch level are applied to all VMs on the vSwitch.
Having Promiscuous Mode enabled means other VMs may be able to sniff traffic going through the Virtual Service Edge.
Zscaler recommends you create and use a port group for your Virtual Service Edge interfaces.

esxi-reverse-path-check.statement: If a vSwitch has multiple physical ports, the ESXi host advanced option Net.ReversePathFwdCheckPromisc must be enabled (set to 1); otherwise multicast traffic loops back to the host, CARP does not function properly, and 'link states coalesced' messages are sent.

quotes: If multiple physical ports exist on the same vSwitch, then the Net.ReversePathFwdCheckPromisc advanced option must be enabled (i.e., set to 1) on the ESXi host.
If it is not, then multicast traffic loops back to the host, causing CARP not to function properly, and "link states coalesced" messages to be sent.

mcls-is-public-se-only.statement: Multi-Cluster Load Sharing is described for Public Service Edge clusters in Zscaler data centers: several clusters in different network address blocks serve the same VIP, so Zscaler can add capacity without customers moving their GRE tunnels.

quotes: The Multi-Cluster Load Sharing feature allows multiple Public Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA) clusters in different network address blocks to participate in a Virtual IP (VIP) address
So, you no longer need to move your GRE tunnels to a new VIP address when a new cluster is added to a DC.

external-lb-recommendation.summary: Whether Zscaler recommends an external load balancer.

quotes: Zscaler does not recommend using external load balancers. However, if your organization must use an external load balancer, see Using an External Load Balancer with Virtual Service Edges.

positions.says: The clusters article says Zscaler does not recommend using external load balancers.

quotes: Clustered Virtual Service Edges Without the Required Switches (Recommended)
Zscaler recommends using the built-in LB.

positions.says: The external load balancer article labels the clustered-without-switches external option "(Recommended)" and also says Zscaler recommends using the built-in LB.

external-lb-recommendation.impact: The two pages agree that the built-in load balancer is preferred; the "(Recommended)" label ranks the two external options against each other, so it should not be read as a recommendation of external over built-in.

external-lb-return-path.title: Return path and source address handling behind an external load balancer
external-lb-return-path.detail: The external load balancer article gives the balancing method, persistence option, forwarding target and probes, but does not say how the return path or the source address is handled behind an external load balancer.
